power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A simulation-based power analysis was conducted in RStudio using the simr package (Green & MacLeod, 2016). Effect sizes for the EMDs and non-EMD comparisons were parameterised based on those reported by Schleinitz et al. (2020). Data were simulated under a GLMM with a subject-level random intercept, and power to detect the vehicle group × speed interaction was assessed using likelihood-ratio tests. Power was estimated using 50 simulations per sample size, with sample size varied from N = 10 to N = 50 and α = .05. The simulations indicated that at least 40 participants were required to achieve adequate power.

text.text: The brief visual window-often only hundreds of milliseconds-in which drivers predict the arrival of oncoming vehicles and decide whether to give way is critical for safe and efficient manoeuvring.
E-mobility devices (EMDs) are a relatively new form of transportation and may challenge these decisions due to their small visual profile and relatively high operating speeds.
Here, we examined whether observers show systematic biases when judging EMDs relative to other common vehicles, potentially contributing to their vulnerability in intersection crashes.

Using naturalistic video stimuli spanning seven vehicle categories, we tested whether observers would overestimate the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs and, consequently, accept smaller gaps for them to pass through an intersection.
Consistent with this prediction, EMDs elicited greater biases in both TTA and gap judgements (N = 31 and N = 59), with these effects further amplified on a visually complex road.

By comparing across vehicle categories under naturalistic viewing conditions, the results provide evidence that the amplified biases observed for EMDs arise from differences in the underlying visual signals available to observers-specifically, their smaller retinal size and potentially less reliable motion cues at higher speeds.

Importantly, these biases were not explained by speed misperception: in a separate two-alternative forced-choice task (N = 49), EMDs were perceived as faster, not slower, than other vehicles at matched speeds.
This dissociation indicates that TTA overestimation cannot be attributed to speed underestimation alone.
Together, these findings link controlled psychophysical processes to real-world traffic behaviour, with implications for future experimental design and traffic safety policy.

E-mobility devices (EMDs), such as e-scooters and e-bikes, are increasingly popular as alternatives to traditional transport in urban and suburban environments (Field & Jon, 2021; Kathiresh et al., 2022; Yannis et al., 2024).

text.text: However, their rapid integration into existing transport systems worldwide has also raised significant safety concerns.

Reports frequently highlight risky practices such as riding without helmets, exceeding speed limits, and operating devices while intoxicated (Bai et al., 2015; Che et al., 2021; Field & Jon, 2021; Useche et al., 2022; Ssi Yan Kai et al., 2024).

A second, less-explored factor concerns how other road users visually perceive these devices.

Compared to larger vehicles, EMDs are smaller, quieter, and less perceptually salient, which may influence how their speed, distance, and arrival time are judged in traffic (Kathiresh et al., 2022; Petzoldt et al., 2017; Schleinitz et al., 2016).

text.text: The current study, therefore, focuses on the perceptual side of the problem by examining how a sample of Australian drivers perform traffic-related visual judgements involving EMDs.
Specifically, we are interested in time-to-arrival (TTA) and gap acceptance tasks.

TTA measures how accurately individuals can predict the arrival time of an approaching vehicle (Lee, 1976; Schiff & Oldak, 1990), whereas gap acceptance measures how much space individuals are comfortable leaving between themselves and oncoming traffic to avoid potential collisions (Alexander et al., 2002; Petzoldt et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2007).

The following sections review the existing literature supporting this account.
Size is an important cue to pictorial distance in human vision: objects closer to the observer are typically perceived as larger, whereas smaller objects are often perceived as farther away.

This can produce the illusion that smaller objects will arrive later than larger ones (Caird & Hancock, 1994; DeLucia et al., 2003; DeLucia & Warren, 1994; Hosking & Crassini, 2011), a phenomenon known as the size-to-arrival effect.

For example, Caird and Hancock (1994) showed that smaller vehicles, such as motorbikes and compact cars, are judged to arrive later than full-size cars and large vans, despite being at the same distance from the observer.

This suggests that the size-based perceptual bias translates to biases in decision-making in traffic contexts.
Crucially, this bias is not tied to the vehicle's categorical label per se.

One possibility is that observers use prior knowledge about the high-speed profile of motorised devices to make more cautious decisions (Davies, 2009; Dey et al., 2019; Schleinitz & Petzoldt, 2019).

text.text: Thus, EMDs may be vulnerable precisely because their motorisation is not always visually obvious.
For example, observers may use visible effort cues, such as pedalling, to infer arrival time (Schleinitz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: For example, observers may use visible effort cues, such as pedalling, to infer arrival time <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Schleinitz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: E-bikes may be particularly prone to misjudgements because they can travel at relatively high speeds, with less visible pedalling effort than conventional bikes.
As a result, observers may underestimate how quickly they are approaching, overestimate TTA, and accept smaller gaps.

Consistent with this account, research has found that e-bikes are consistently judged to arrive later than conventional bikes, and controlling for pedalling frequency seems to reduce their perceived TTA difference (Schleinitz et al., 2016).

text.text: However, these effects may depend on the speed range tested.

A follow-up study by Schleinitz et al. (2020) found no reliable difference in TTA estimates or gap judgements between e-bikes and conventional bikes when the tested speed range was 25 to 35 km/h, rather than 10 to 25 km/h in their previous research (Schleinitz et al., 2016).

(2020)</ref> found no reliable difference in TTA estimates or gap judgements between e-bikes and conventional bikes when the tested speed range was 25 to 35 km/h, rather than 10 to 25 km/h in their previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Schleinitz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: E-scooters, however, were given larger gaps than both e-bikes and conventional bicycles, which the authors suggested may reflect greater novelty associated with these vehicles.

Together, these findings suggest that although their high-speed operation may contribute to perceptual biases specific to EMDs, these effects appear to depend on the cues available to observers and the speed range tested.

This leaves open the question of exactly how the different speed and size profiles associated with these vehicles in everyday traffic might affect drivers' perception, a question the current research addresses.
The first aim of the current study was to examine whether EMDs' small size influences perceived arrival time and gap acceptance.
To our knowledge, no previous research has compared EMDs across a range of everyday vehicle types that differ in visual size.
Because EMDs are among the smallest vehicle categories encountered in traffic, we expected observers to exhibit a larger perceptual bias in their responses to these vehicles.

Specifically, EMDs would be judged to arrive later (i.e., with greater TTA overestimation) and would be given smaller gaps than larger vehicles, but to a similar extent as other small vehicles (e.g., motorbikes).
To test this, we compared two EMDs (e-scooter and e-bike) with three larger vehicle types (cars, SUVs, and trucks) and included other small vehicles (bikes and motorbikes) for comparison.
To enhance ecological validity, we used recorded video stimuli rather than the computer-generated simulations used in prior research.
This allowed observers to respond under more natural visual conditions, in which cues such as vehicle appearance, lighting, and motion vary as they do in real traffic environments.
Second, as discussed above, speed-related EMD biases depend on the cues observers use and on the speed ranges tested across studies.
Because the current study examines drivers' perception under naturalistic conditions, we do not make specific assumptions about which cues participants will rely on.
Instead, we allow participants to make judgments as they would in real traffic contexts, and then examine whether the resulting pattern is more consistent with one explanation or another.

To address the inconsistent findings across speed ranges identified in previous studies (Schleinitz et al., 2016 (Schleinitz et al., , 2020)), we examined a broader operating range, from 5 to 35 km/h, in finer 5 km/h increments.

text.text: This allowed us to test whether EMD bias changed systematically with speed, rather than comparing its influence across discrete speed categories, as in previous research.

Given that motion estimation is often less reliable at higher speeds, we expected higher vehicle approach speeds to increase the TTA overestimation, a result typically reported in traffic and perception literature (Petzoldt et al., 2017; Schleinitz et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2001).

text.text: Note that we do not make specific predictions about the direction of the gap bias as a function of speed for these vehicles.
If observers judge the EMDs as arriving later but nevertheless accept larger gaps, this suggests that higher speeds increase caution toward these vehicles.

In contrast, if observers judge the EMDs as arriving later and accept smaller gaps, this will indicate a potentially hazardous perceptual misjudgement: observers may behave as though less space is needed because the arrival of the vehicle appears less imminent than it actually is.

To maximise ecological validity while maintaining experimental control, we recorded stimuli on a closed-circuit track at the Royal Automobile Club of Queensland (RACQ) Mobility Centre using a Sony AX53 camera (1080p, 60fps).
Videos were recorded at two locations on the track: (1) a downhill, long-distance approach and (2) a short-distance approach around a corner.
Examples of the two locations are provided in Supplementary Material E. The camera was positioned from a driver's point of view, in the left-hand lane of a two-way road.
In each video, a vehicle travelled toward the camera in the right-hand lane at a controlled speed.
Videos were trimmed from the vehicle's first full visibility to its complete exit from frame.
The approaching vehicle was one of seven types: a bike, e-scooter, e-bike, motorbike, car, SUV, or truck.
Approach speeds varied in 5km/h increments: 5-30km/h for the bike; 5-35km/h for the e-scooters and e-bike; and from 10-60km/h for the motorbike, car, SUV, and truck.
For the e-scooter, two videos were available at every speed, each featuring a different rider.
The riders were similarly dressed in black and were comparable in height and body size.
In the main experiment, e-scooter trials were randomly drawn from these two videos and therefore featured either rider.
Two riders were also used for the bike stimuli, although this variation was limited to the 10 km/h condition because filming at that speed required additional assistance.
Thus, rider identity was not systematically associated with vehicle type or varied across the full range of bike speeds.

All vehicle-speed combinations were recorded twice at each location (i.e., two videos per vehicle x speed x location) with the following exceptions: the bike was only recorded at Location 1 and only up to 30km/hr due to a tyre failure, the e-scooters at Location 2 could only reach 30km/hr without the steep downhill approach, and for all vehicle speeds above 50km/hr could not be achieved at Location 2 due to the corner approach.
Since the videos were filmed outdoors, lighting conditions could not be experimentally controlled.
To minimise variability, all videos were recorded on the same day between mid-morning and mid-afternoon.
Camera settings were kept consistent across recordings, and for each vehicle x speed x location combination, the clip with the most consistent lighting was selected.
This resulted in a total of 124 videos to be used in the experiments.
Speed was measured with a Bushnell Velocity Speed Gun (Model 101911) and crossvalidated against each vehicle's speedometer.
Due to the 15km/hr detection limit of the speed gun, 5 and 10km/hr speeds were recorded from the speedometer only.
Across overlapping speeds, the recording methods differed by ≤3km/hr.

Our first experiment examined the influence of vehicle size and speed on time-to-arrival (TTA) estimation.

Based on the size-arrival effect, we hypothesised that e-mobility devices (EMDs; e-scooters and e-bikes) would show greater TTA overestimation than larger vehicles, meaning that observers would judge EMDs as arriving later than larger vehicles.
However, we expected this bias to be comparable in magnitude to that observed for other small vehicles.
We also hypothesised that higher approach speeds would increase TTA estimates.
A total of 45 participants completed Experiment 1.

However, five were removed due to unexpected technical difficulties (e.g., experiments stopped due to software updates), and another five were removed due to performance deviations from the mean (more than 2 standard deviations).
This resulted in a final sample of 35 participants (25 women, 10 men, aged 18-40, Mage = 21.29) for the statistical analysis.
They took, on average, 1 hour and 26 minutes to complete the experiment.
An 'arrival point' (yellow line) was digitally superimposed over the road surface of each video.
The original videos were cut to end when the leading edge of the vehicle reached the arrival point.
The experiment was a within-subjects design with prediction windows (3 levels: 1, 2, and 3 seconds) x vehicle type (7 levels: bike, e-scooter, e-bike, motorbike, car, SUV, truck) x speed.
Speed levels varied by vehicle type (see General Method), resulting in a non-factorial design.

text.text: This pattern suggests a potential mechanism underlying risky decisions at intersections: when drivers must make rapid judgements based on briefly unfolding approach information, they may overestimate the time available before an approaching EMD arrives, increasing the likelihood of accepting less safe gaps.
Experiment 2 builds on this account by directly examining gap acceptance behaviour.
Experiment 1 showed that participants overestimated the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs relative to larger vehicles, consistent with the size-to-arrival effect.
Notably, this overestimation increased with speed, and did so more strongly for EMDs than for other vehicle types.
This raises an important question: do these perceptual biases influence decision-making?
To address this, Experiment 2 examined how vehicle type and speed influence gap acceptance judgments.
If the perceptual biases observed in Experiment 1 carry over into behaviour, participants should accept smaller gaps for EMDs compared to other vehicles.

The response window began at video onset.

Participants pressed the brake pedal, depicted using the vector artwork by Borodin (n.d.), when they judged that it would no longer be safe to initiate a right-hand turn in front of the oncoming vehicle.
Upon responding, the indicator turned red for 150ms to confirm that the response had been registered.

We showed participants (N = 55) video clips of seven vehicle types, including the EMDs, and asked them to signal stop when they deemed it no longer safe to initiate a crossing of the intersection in front of the oncoming vehicle.

The dependent variable, gap acceptance, was defined relative to the time the vehicle reached the intersection, with positive values indicating that participants accepted a gap before the vehicle arrived and negative values indicating a late decision.
On average, participants accepted gaps that allowed vehicles to pass safely (M = 5.67 s, SD = 5.22), confirming that the task was performed as intended.
However, gap acceptance varied systematically across vehicle types.

As shown in Figure 7, responses for e-bikes and e-scooters exhibited a broader spread across both positive and negative ranges than those of other vehicles, indicating greater variability in gap judgements.

Importantly, we found that EMDs showed the steepest decline in the gap selected as speed increased, indicating that the combined effects of speed and small size might disproportionately influence perceptual judgements involving these devices, similarly to our Experiment 1.
Notably, this effect was most pronounced on the curved road (Road 2), suggesting that EMDs are particularly susceptible to miscalibrated gap selection under increased environmental uncertainty.

Importantly, the reduced gap acceptance observed here aligns with the increased overestimation of time-to-arrival for EMDs at higher speeds in Experiment 1, suggesting that speed-related perceptual biases may underlie EMD misjudgements.

To test this possibility, Experiment 3 examined speed perception directly, with the hypothesis that EMDs would be underestimated in speed, given the inverse relationship between speed and time-to-arrival.
Experiments 1 and 2 showed that EMDs are systematically misjudged in both time-toarrival (TTA) and gap acceptance tasks, with these biases strongly modulated by speed.
This raises the possibility that speed perception itself may be distorted for EMDs.

Because TTA is inversely related to perceived speed, the overestimation of TTA for EMDs that we observed in Experiment 1 would predict that EMDs are perceived as travelling more slowly than they actually are.
Accordingly, we hypothesised that, in a two-alternative forced-choice task (2AFC), participants would underestimate the speed of EMDs relative to other vehicles.
To keep the design manageable and limit the number of pairwise comparisons, the e-scooter was used as the reference vehicle.
Forty-one participants (33 women, 8 men) aged 18-49 years (M = 22.88, SD = 7.44) completed Experiment 3.
On average, participants took 1 hour and 7 minutes to complete the experiment.
All participants' data were retained to ensure adequate statistical power.
The stimuli were 2000ms snippets extracted from each video.
To prevent the vehicle's starting position from cuing its speed, the snippet began at a randomly selected point 6.5, 7, or 7.5 seconds before the end of the original video.
If a video was too short to accommodate this window, the snippet began at the start of the original video.
Participants completed a 2AFC speed-discrimination task, indicating whether the vehicle in the first or second clip was travelling faster (using the left or right arrow keys).
Each trial paired an e-scooter (reference vehicle) with a comparison vehicle selected from six types: bike, e-bike, motorbike, car, SUV, or truck.
The speed difference ratio between the two vehicles ranged from one (identical) to three (one vehicle travelled at three times the speed of the other).
Trials in which the comparison speed exceeded this threefold range were excluded to avoid extreme and potentially uninformative comparisons.
This design yielded 252 unique vehicle pairing x e-scooter speed x comparison vehicle speed combinations.
Each combination was presented twice for a total of 504 trials.

Each trial began with a 500ms re-orientation period displaying a blank grey screen, followed by two 2000ms clips of an approaching vehicle or road user, separated by a 500ms inter-trial interval of a blank grey screen.
After the second clip, a 500ms post-stimulus blank screen was shown, after which the response prompt appeared, and the response window commenced.
Participants indicated whether the vehicle in the first (left arrow key) or second (right arrow key) clip was travelling faster (speeded response).
They were asked to respond as accurately as possible.
Raw participant responses were recoded as binary outcomes (1 = e-scooter judged faster,0 = comparison vehicle judged faster).
This transformation allowed us to visualise the probability of choosing the reference vehicle (e-scooter) across all vehicle comparisons (Figure 12).

text.text: Then, to formally quantify bias toward the reference vehicle, we fitted a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) with a probit link function under a binomial distribution.
The model included fixed effects of speed difference (Δspeed = e-scooter -comparison vehicle), vehicle type (categorical), and their interaction.
Random intercepts were included to account for subject-level variability.
The probit link maps the linear predictor onto the cumulative Gaussian distribution, allowing model predictions to be interpreted as cumulative normal psychometric functions.
Bias was quantified using the point of subjective equality (PSE), defined as the speed at which the predicted probability of judging the e-scooter as faster equalled 0.5.
Because the model used a probit link, this corresponds to the value of speed at which the linear predictor equals zero.
For each vehicle type, the PSE was thus computed analytically from the model's fixed-effect intercept and slope parameters.
The full model equation is provided in the Supplementary Material B.

Our third experiment examined participants' speed judgments of e-scooters relative to six other common road vehicles (e-bike, bike, motorbike, car, SUV, truck) in a two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) task.
On average, participants achieved 70.73% accuracy (N = 41), indicating they could determine above chance whether the e-scooter or the comparison vehicle was travelling faster.
We calculated the proportion of trials in which participants selected the escooter as the faster vehicle, which served as the dependent variable.
Descriptive results were visualised in a heatmap (Figure 12), with brighter yellow indicating a higher likelihood of selecting the e-scooter and darker magenta/purple indicating a lower likelihood.
text.formatted: Descriptive results were visualised in a heatmap (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">12</ref>), with brighter yellow indicating a higher likelihood of selecting the e-scooter and darker magenta/purple indicating a lower likelihood.

text.text: The dense cluster of yellow pixels in the top-left corner of the heatmaps suggests that when e-scooters were travelling faster than their comparison vehicles (as indicated by the speed difference between the x-and y-axes), participants were more likely to choose the e-scooter, confirming that they performed the task as instructed.
To address our main hypothesis, we examined whether participants overestimated or underestimated the speed of e-scooters relative to other vehicles.
In a 2AFC task, bias is reflected in a systematic preference for one option when both vehicles are objectively moving at the same speed.
In Figure 12, the diagonal dashed line represents objective equality (e.g., e-scooter at 10 km/h vs. car at 10 km/h).

text.text: The irregular line connects points of subjective equality, indicating the speed combinations participants perceived as equally fast.
The separation between these two lines reflects perceptual bias.
In the car-e-scooter comparison, the subjective equality line was consistently shifted to the right of the objective equality line.

This indicates that the car had to be physically faster than the e-scooter to be judged as equally fast, demonstrating a systematic overestimation of e-scooter speed, contrary to our initial hypothesis.
Other vehicle comparisons showed a similar tendency to overestimate the e-scooter's speed, although these effects were less consistent.
In these cases, the subjective equality lines fluctuated around the objective equality line rather than remaining cleanly on one side.

To formally quantify bias in speed judgement in a within-subjects experiment, we generated psychometric functions for each vehicle comparison by fitting a generalised linear mixed-effects model (GLMM).
Responses were recoded as binary (1 = e-scooter judged faster,0 = comparison vehicle judged faster).
Fixed effects included vehicle type and speed difference, and individual differences were modelled with a nested random-effects structure.
The results of this model yielded significant coefficients for speed and for all vehicle comparisons (Supplementary Material B).

We adopted a probit link function corresponding to the cumulative Gaussian distribution under a binomial structure, allowing model predictions to be interpreted as psychometric functions (Figure 13a).
text.formatted: We adopted a probit link function corresponding to the cumulative Gaussian distribution under a binomial structure, allowing model predictions to be interpreted as psychometric functions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">13a</ref>).

text.text: Two properties were of key interest: the slopes of these functions, which indicate discriminability, and the horizontal shifts of the functions, which indicate bias.
To quantify the slopes of the psychometric functions for each vehicle comparison, we extracted the model coefficients for vehicle effects as a function of speed difference.
Higher values indicate steeper slopes and greater sensitivity in discriminating speed differences between the e-scooter and the comparison vehicle.

Across vehicle types, the average slope of speed difference was β = 0.85, p < .01, indicating that a one-unit increase in speed difference (equivalent to 14 km/h in raw units due to rescaling of speed) produced a substantial increase in the latent decision variable favouring the escooter.

text.text: Under a probit link, this slope corresponds to a just-noticeable difference of approximately 11 km/h (50%-75% criterion).
That is, participants required a speed difference of about 11 km/h to discriminate the speeds of the two vehicles with 75% accuracy.
Each vehicle's slope differed significantly from the grand mean reported above (all p < 0.01).

text.text: Among the comparison vehicles, those of similar size to the e-scooter showed greater discriminability.
The bike had the steepest slope, with a positive deviation from the grand mean (β = 0.44), indicating greater-than-average discriminability.
This was followed by the e-bike (β = 0.24).
In contrast, larger vehicles showed reduced discriminability, as reflected in negative deviations from the grand mean (-0.12 to-0.26).
The car had the shallowest slope (β = -0.26), indicating the weakest discrimination performance.

Overall, these results roughly follow a sizebased pattern in discriminability: participants were more sensitive to speed differences between the e-scooter and smaller vehicles than between the e-scooter and larger vehicles.
The model coefficients were then used to derive the point of subjective equality (PSE), providing a quantitative measure of participants' speed bias (Methods).
The PSE was defined as the difference between the objectively matched speed level (Sdiff = 0) and the speed level at which participants responded at chance (50%).

This pattern suggests that participants judged comparison vehicles to be travelling at the same speed as the e-scooter, when the e-scooter was objectively slower, reflecting an overall overestimation of e-scooter speed.

Contrary to our expectations, the 2AFC speed-judgement experiment revealed that escooters were perceived as faster, not slower, than most vehicles, even when their actual speeds were matched.

This finding suggests that speed perception may not directly align with the mechanisms underlying time-to-arrival and gap judgement observed in the earlier experiments, given that overestimating time-to-arrival would imply underestimating speed.

Instead, these results are consistent with the size-speed illusion literature (Clark et al., 2016; Lee & Sheppard, 2017; Yong & Hsieh, 2017), which suggests that smaller vehicles are perceived as moving faster than larger ones at the same physical speed.

text.text: A key question, therefore, is how safely these devices can be integrated into existing traffic systems.

Using naturalistic video stimuli, the present study investigated whether basic visual cues associated with e-scooters and e-bikes influence observers' perception of time-to-arrival and, consequently, their gap decision-making.
A follow-up experiment then explored whether differences between vehicles' TTA estimates and gap acceptance may be explained by differences in speed perception.

Smaller vehicles are often perceived as farther away, leading drivers to overestimate their time-to-arrival and select shorter gaps to allow them to pass an intersection (Caird & Hancock, 1994; DeLucia et al., 2003; DeLucia & Warren, 1994; Horswill et al., 2005).

text.text: Consistent with this size-arrival effect, EMDs were systematically misjudged to arrive later than larger vehicles and were assigned smaller gaps.

This pattern aligns with our hypothesis and prior findings (Caird & Hancock, 1994; DeLucia et al., 2003; DeLucia & Warren, 1994; Horswill et al., 2005), suggesting that the smaller visual angles subtended by these vehicles may increase their susceptibility to timing misjudgements and, in turn, reduce the safety margins allocated to them.

text.text: Importantly, these effects were observed when viewing naturalistic stimuli, supporting the ecological validity of vehicle size effects beyond those observed in driving simulations (Caird & Hancock, 1994; Levulis et al., 2015; Sidaway et al., 1996).

text.text: Both time-to-arrival (TTA) and gap selection errors increased disproportionately for EMDs at higher speeds, with greater TTA overestimation and reduced gap acceptance, rising more steeply than for larger vehicles and even for similarly sized smaller vehicles such as bikes and motorbikes.
This suggests that higher speeds amplify the existing biases associated with EMDs, beyond the contribution of size alone.
This finding broadly aligns with previous research highlighting the potential risks of higher speeds associated with EMDs (Petzoldt et al., 2017; Schleinitz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This finding broadly aligns with previous research highlighting the potential risks of higher speeds associated with EMDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Petzoldt et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Schleinitz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this work in two important ways: first, by testing a wider, more finely sampled range of approach speeds; and second, by comparing EMDs against multiple everyday vehicles of different physical sizes.

This allowed us to show that the speed-related reduction in accepted gaps was not only present for e-bikes, as in Petzoldt et al. (2017), but also extended to e-scooters, and was especially pronounced for EMDs relative to the other common road vehicles.

text.text: Importantly, we also found that higher speeds were associated with greater TTA overestimation for EMDs relative to other vehicles.
This suggests that the speed-related reduction in accepted gaps has a perceptual basis: riskier crossing decisions were accompanied by greater overestimation of the vehicles' TTA.
This interpretation is consistent with Petzoldt et al. (2014), who showed that pedestrian crossing decisions were predicted by biases in participants' TTA estimates.

text.text: Overall, these results suggest that high-speed operation may make EMDs especially vulnerable to risky road-user decisions.
Two accounts have been proposed to explain why EMDs may be perceived or judged differently at higher speeds.
One account suggests that EMDs may be treated as motorised, highspeed vehicles, leading to more cautious gap decisions.

For example, Schleinitz and Petzoldt (2019) found that observers gave larger gaps to riders when cues indicated the vehicle was an ebike than when cues indicated it was a conventional bike, even though the same vehicle was used, suggesting that recognising a vehicle as motorised may encourage more cautious decisions.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Schleinitz and Petzoldt (2019)</ref> found that observers gave larger gaps to riders when cues indicated the vehicle was an ebike than when cues indicated it was a conventional bike, even though the same vehicle was used, suggesting that recognising a vehicle as motorised may encourage more cautious decisions.

text.text: Our findings are consistent with this interpretation: EMDs were generally associated with larger accepted gaps than conventional bikes.
This suggests that, even without explicit labelling, observers may use motorisation to adjust their gap judgements and compensate for the potential risks associated with these vehicles.
However, our results also showed that this behavioural adjustment may not be consistent across speeds.
Although EMDs received relatively cautious gap responses at lower speeds, this benefit appeared to decrease more sharply with increasing speed than conventional bikes.
This suggests that attempts to give more gap for these devices might not sufficiently scale up as speed increases.

Our study, therefore, expands on past studies (Schleinitz et al., 2020; Schleinitz & Petzoldt, 2019), showing that while observers' gap judgement may reflect considering motorisation, this does not necessarily make EMDs safer on the road.
text.formatted: Our study, therefore, expands on past studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Schleinitz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Schleinitz & Petzoldt, 2019)</ref>, showing that while observers' gap judgement may reflect considering motorisation, this does not necessarily make EMDs safer on the road.

text.text: In fact, this may be especially problematic because observers may not be able to maintain a consistent gap for these vehicles as speed increases compared to others.
A separate account is that visible pedalling provides a cue to approach speed.

Under this account, pedalling may help observers estimate the speed of conventional bikes, but may provide a weaker or less reliable cue for e-bikes when motorisation is not obvious (Schleinitz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Under this account, pedalling may help observers estimate the speed of conventional bikes, but may provide a weaker or less reliable cue for e-bikes when motorisation is not obvious <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Schleinitz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, we did not find evidence that e-bikes were systematically overestimated relative to conventional bicycles.

Although the difference in perceived TTA between the two vehicle types appeared to increase at higher speeds, the three-way interaction was largely driven by a single prediction-window condition (1 s), in which perceived TTA for bicycles decreased as speed increased.
This pattern may partly reflect uncontrolled stimulus-level variation arising from our decision to preserve natural variability across the filmed approaches.
Further research using more tightly controlled stimuli is needed to determine whether the observed pattern reflects a genuine vehicle-specific effect or incidental differences in stimulus properties.
Could this speed-dependent effect be driven by a misjudgement of vehicle speed specific to EMDs?
In our third experiment, we initially hypothesised that the speed-dependent biases for EMDs in TTA and gap judgements might arise from underestimating their speed.
This prediction follows the inverse relationship between time and speed (i.e., time-to-arrival = distance/speed).
Under this account, observers would perceive EMDs as travelling more slowly than they actually are, leading to inflated time-to-arrival estimates and smaller gaps.
However, we found the opposite pattern: e-scooters were overestimated in speed relative to most larger vehicles, with this effect attenuated compared with similarly sized small vehicles.

This result again highlights the influence of size and is consistent with previous findings on the size-speed illusion (Clark et al., 2016; Petzoldt, 2016; Yong & Hsieh, 2017), whereby smaller objects are perceived as moving faster than larger ones.
text.formatted: This result again highlights the influence of size and is consistent with previous findings on the size-speed illusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Clark et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Petzoldt, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Yong & Hsieh, 2017)</ref>, whereby smaller objects are perceived as moving faster than larger ones.

text.text: Nevertheless, if our observers had relied on this bias when making time-to-arrival judgements, they should have underestimated, rather than overestimated, the time-to-arrival of EMDs relative to larger vehicles (Petzoldt, 2016).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, if our observers had relied on this bias when making time-to-arrival judgements, they should have underestimated, rather than overestimated, the time-to-arrival of EMDs relative to larger vehicles <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Petzoldt, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, in our experiment, the overestimation of EMD TTA increased with speed, regardless of relative vehicle size, suggesting that a simple size-based account may be insufficient.
The observed dissociation, therefore, suggests that time-to-arrival errors for EMDs cannot be fully explained by speed misjudgement alone.
Previous work has shown that environmental factors can influence gap selection, with steeper road gradients leading to smaller accepted gaps for EMDs (Petzoldt et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Previous work has shown that environmental factors can influence gap selection, with steeper road gradients leading to smaller accepted gaps for EMDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Petzoldt et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Extending this work, we found that, compared to steep straight-road contexts, curved-road contexts elicited the most pronounced reduction in accepted gaps for EMDs.
In this condition, vehicles emerged from a bend rather than remaining continuously visible, likely increasing visual uncertainty about their approach dynamics.
This sensitivity to environmental uncertainty may have important implications for realworld traffic contexts.

Detecting and tracking EMDs may become more difficult, for example, when they are partially occluded by larger vehicles or under low-visibility conditions such as at night (Gould et al., 2012; Kennon et al., 2025; Lacherez et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Detecting and tracking EMDs may become more difficult, for example, when they are partially occluded by larger vehicles or under low-visibility conditions such as at night <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gould et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kennon et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lacherez et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Future experiments could therefore examine how occlusion affects EMD perception, particularly because these vehicles may appear unexpectedly from peripheral locations or around corners in dense urban areas (Inquiry into e-mobility safety and use in Queensland, 2026).
More broadly, examining how visibility, occlusion, and road complexity interact with EMD motion processing could help identify strategies for reducing risk.
Potential interventions include warning signage, restrictions on EMD use in certain road environments, or design changes that improve visual conspicuity.
Research on motorbike safety, for instance, shows that adding auxiliary side headlights can significantly reduce unsafe gap-selection behaviour (Cavallo et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Research on motorbike safety, for instance, shows that adding auxiliary side headlights can significantly reduce unsafe gap-selection behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cavallo et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The present study contributes to understanding how environmental factors shape perceptual biases in EMD-related driving decisions.
We showed that people overestimate the time-to-arrival and may consequently afford smaller gaps to EMDs.
Two factors underpinned this effect: size and speed.

Examining them in real-world traffic videos, our findings support the notion that the small size of EMDs and their relatively high-speed profiles increase their susceptibility to perceptual and decisional biases, which, in turn, could contribute to their on-road vulnerability.
We also found evidence that road complexity modulates these effects, indicating that environmental factors further amplify their existing vulnerabilities.
Several limitations should be considered.

First, although we found that overestimation of time-to-arrival coincided with smaller accepted gaps for EMDs, and that both effects were strongly moderated by speed, these results were obtained from separate participant groups.
Establishing a direct link between perception and behaviour would require a repeated-measures design that relates individual performance across both tasks (Petzoldt, 2014).
text.formatted: Establishing a direct link between perception and behaviour would require a repeated-measures design that relates individual performance across both tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Petzoldt, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, the current study provides empirical evidence of similar patterns of time-to-arrival bias and gap selection for EMDs (Petzoldt, 2016 (Petzoldt, , 2016;; Schleinitz et al., 2016 Schleinitz et al., , 2020)).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the current study provides empirical evidence of similar patterns of time-to-arrival bias and gap selection for EMDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Petzoldt, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Petzoldt, , 2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Schleinitz et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schleinitz et al., , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: A second limitation concerns stimulus properties.
Smaller vehicles in our dataset (ebikes, e-scooters, and bikes) were generally darker in colour than larger vehicles, which were predominantly white.

Because higher contrast is associated with faster perceived speed, this difference may have contributed to some of the observed size-based effects (Rideaux & Welchman, 2020; Sudkamp & Souto, 2023; Yong & Hsieh, 2017).
text.formatted: Because higher contrast is associated with faster perceived speed, this difference may have contributed to some of the observed size-based effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rideaux & Welchman, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Sudkamp & Souto, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Yong & Hsieh, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, the aim of the present study was not to control for such variability, but to examine how naturally occurring visual differences in real-world driving environments shape perception and behaviour.
The darker appearance of EMDs in our stimuli reflects the typical characteristics of privately owned devices encountered in everyday traffic.
Future work could extend this approach by including other commonly encountered EMDs, such as rental devices, which often feature brighter colours to enhance visibility.
Comparing these conditions would help determine the extent to which the biases observed here generalise.

From a policy perspective, our findings highlight that the misperception of EMDs is disproportionately affected by speed, with judgements becoming increasingly dangerous compared to other vehicles as speed increases.
These results provide empirical support for policies that limit the speed of EMDs to improve safety.
Additionally, our results suggest this effect of speed is further exaggerated in environments where the visibility of an approaching EMD is limited (e.g., Road 2).

In real-world road environments, approaching vehicles are often only partially visible, such as when they are travelling in blind spots, emerging from behind parked cars, or occluded by other road users or roadside infrastructure.
Taken together, these findings suggest that EMDs may be disproportionately vulnerable on the road.
Our findings highlight the importance of designing interventions that account for perceptual limitations in judging EMDs.

For instance, improving the visual conspicuity of EMDs, regulating their speeds in high-risk environments, and adapting road infrastructure to enhance visibility and predictability may help mitigate these biases and improve safety outcomes.
With the increasing presence of autonomous systems, it is also important to consider how human perceptual biases interact with machine decision-making (Hubmann et al., 2017).
text.formatted: With the increasing presence of autonomous systems, it is also important to consider how human perceptual biases interact with machine decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hubmann et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Systems that account for the greater uncertainty associated with EMDs-for example, by adopting more conservative gap-acceptance thresholds-may reduce the risk of unsafe interactions with vulnerable road users.

text.text: Psychometric Curve Fitting using GLMM A generalised linear mixed effects model was fitted to estimate the probability of selecting 'escooter' as a function of the predictor variables.

The model equation considered fixed effects of signed speed difference (Sdiff), compared vehicle type (ComparedVehicle), and their interaction, while treating individual variance as a random effect, allowed to vary across fixed effects (1|ID).
Taking the inverse of the cumulative normal distribution (Φ -1 ), the linear equation is thus:
To allow for meaningful comparison with the binary task response data from the regression, the Sdiff scores were rescaled as z-scores (Sdiff_s) when running the model in R Studio.
To confirm that including individual variance as a random effect improved the model, an alternative that excluded this was compared.
Model fit was assessed using Akaike's information criterion (AIC).
The model, including participant ID as a random effect (AIC = 17075), provided a better fit than the model that did not account for individual variance (AIC = 17411).
Therefore, the model including individual variance was selected for analysis.
Sigmoidal psychometric functions with a cumulative normal distribution were then generated from the model for each vehicle comparison.
Curves were fitted for each participant, and then the group average was calculated.
The fitted psychometric functions were used to estimate both individual and grouplevel points of subjective equality (PSE) for each vehicle comparison.
In the probit model, the PSE corresponds to the value of signed speed difference (Sdiff) at which the probability of selecting the e-scooter equals 0.5.

Because the fitted model included random intercepts but not random slopes, the slope remained a group-level estimate.

Objective equality was defined as Sdiff = 0 km/h, corresponding to the condition in which the e-scooter and the comparison vehicle moved at the same physical speed.
Deviations of the PSE from zero, therefore, indicate systematic perceptual bias.
Specifically, the sign and magnitude of the PSE reflect both the direction and extent to which the perceived speed of the e-scooter differs from that of the comparison vehicle.
Because the PSE is expressed in units of Sdiff, it is reported in kilometres per hour.
Using the same fixed-and random-effects structure, we fitted an additional model to predict participants' accepted spatial distance.
Spatial distance was derived by multiplying the reported temporal gap by vehicle speed and converting the result to meters.

This transformation does not assume veridical speed perception; rather, it provides a mathematical conversion that expresses time-based judgements in spatial units, enabling direct comparison with physical clearance distances that would otherwise be difficult to estimate from naturalistic scene videos.
Full model coefficients are reported in the Supplementary Material A.

Nevertheless, the systematic speed effect indicates that participants' responses did not collapse spatial clearance at higher speeds but instead resulted in larger accepted physical gaps.
